steps.body: Feed every input to |x| and plot the results. Inputs on the right rise along y = x. Inputs on the left are negative, but their DISTANCES are positive, so the left half rises too — mirror-imaging the right. Two rising branches meeting at the origin: a V.
Plot one point on the left branch.

widget.prompt: On y = |x|, plot the point where x = −2.

pointErrors.feedback: That would say |−2| = 0 — that −2 sits ON zero. It sits two units away, so the height is 2.
Correct height, wrong branch: that is x = +2. The left branch is where the mirror argument does its work.

widget.missFeedback: |−2| is the distance from −2 to 0, which is 2. So the point is (−2, 2).
widget.successFeedback: (−2, 2): two units left of zero, plotted two units UP. The left branch climbs as x moves away from the origin.

predict.prompt: y = |x| at x = −2 — where does the point land?

options.label: Two BELOW the axis — negative input, negative height
On the axis — the negative cancels

predict.reveal: Heights on this graph are distances, and distances are never negative. That single fact forces the left half upward and makes the V — the graph can touch the x-axis but can never dip below it.

explanationVariants: The smallest possible distance is 0, reached only at x = 0, so the vertex sits at (0, 0).
Every other input is some positive distance from zero, so nothing on the graph dips below the origin.

widget.prompt: What is the LOWEST point on y = |x|?

options.label: (0, 0) — the vertex
options.feedback: Yes: distance 0 happens exactly once, at the origin, and nothing can beat it.

options.label: There is none — it goes down forever
options.feedback: That is true of y = x, not y = |x|. Distances have a floor at 0.
|−1| = 1, so that point is (−1, 1) — above the axis, not below.

steps.body: The corner is the signature. A line has one constant slope; the V has two — it falls at slope −1 until the origin, then climbs at slope +1. The switch happens exactly where the inside of the bars changes sign, and that is the vertex.

explanationVariants: |−4| = 4, so the point at x = −4 has height 4.
Four units from zero means a height of four, no matter which side.

widget.prompt: On y = |x|, what is y when x = −4?

commonErrors.feedback: Heights on the V are distances — they never go negative. |−4| = 4.
Zero height happens only at the vertex, x = 0.

widget.successFeedback: 4 — and (4, 4) sits at the same height on the right branch. Mirror images.

explanationVariants: |−3| = 3 = |3|, so the two points sit at the same height.
Inputs that are mirror images across 0 have equal distances, hence equal heights.

widget.prompt: On y = |x|, compare the heights at x = −3 and x = 3.

options.label: Equal — both 3
options.feedback: Exactly: the V is symmetric about the y-axis because |−a| = |a|.

options.label: The x = 3 point is higher
options.feedback: Both distances are 3. Nothing about the right side makes it taller.

options.label: The x = −3 point is lower, at −3
options.feedback: That would put the graph below the axis, which distance forbids.

explanationVariants: Height 6 needs distance 6, and two inputs are six units from 0: 6 and −6.
A horizontal line at y = 6 cuts the V once on each branch.
hints: Sketch the horizontal line y = 6 across the V.
Count how many times that line meets the graph — the V has two branches.
It meets the right branch at x = 6 and the left branch at x = −6.

widget.prompt: How many points on y = |x| have height exactly 6?

commonErrors.feedback: One is the answer for a straight line. The V climbs on BOTH sides of the vertex, so a horizontal line above the vertex hits it twice.
That is the height, not the count. The qualifying inputs are x = 6 and x = −6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: y = 6 meets the V twice — at x = 6 and x = −6.
widget.successFeedback: Two — every height above the vertex is reached twice, which is exactly why |x| = 6 will have two solutions.

takeaways: y = |x| is a V: slope −1 into the vertex, slope +1 out of it.
The vertex (0, 0) is the graph's floor — distance cannot go below zero.
Mirror-image inputs have equal heights, so heights above the vertex are hit twice.
steps.teaser: Next: move that V around — and find out which direction a minus sign inside the bars really pushes it.
